\paragraph{F7: Full-pathway gradient stopping shows mixed results.}
Exp\_018 applies Selective Gradient Stopping (SGS) by detaching all non-KL gradients from $e_{\dt}$; this blocks the observation decoder pathway identified in F2 as the primary CIVO conduit. Figure~\ref{fig:civo_decomposition} decomposes evaluation returns across conditions. Trained $\dt$-embedding alone produces $-73\%$ peak and $-86\%$ final eval degradation relative to the baseline. Full-SGS seed~1 avoids collapse (eval \sgseval{}, $-51\%$ final relative to baseline) while seed~2 collapses (eval 40.8, $-96\%$); the overall recovery rate is 50\%. SGS reduces but does not eliminate CIVO risk: the gradient pathway it blocks is necessary but not sufficient for reliable elimination. Reward-only SGS (016e) fails entirely (NVE $10.42\times$). Cross-environment validation on Cheetah Run (010b) confirms CIVO generalization: evaluation peaks at 321.9 before declining to 51.7 at 105K ($-84\%$, minimum 22.7 at 65K); peak NVE $8.27\times$. Full-SGS on Cheetah Run enables recovery from transient CIVO onset (NVE $9.94\times$ at 45K, eval 4.6) to functional performance (eval 221.5 at 105K), in contrast to permanent collapse without SGS (010b: eval 51.7). Combined with Walker results (50\% recovery rate), SGS is necessary but not sufficient for CIVO elimination. Removing the embedding on Cheetah eliminates CIVO entirely (024b, 2 seeds, NVE $< 0.2\times$, eval 96.5/77.3), replicating the Walker causal control (008f) in a second environment.
